subtitle: Everything at once: reporting, passive and position
words.intro: A German talk show has a round table, five guests, a host who lets everybody finish and a word for the moment nobody does: *Streitkultur*, the culture of arguing. It’s considered a good thing.

grammar[0].subheading: Getting in, staying in, and answering back politely
grammar[0].blocks[0].title: In a discussion
grammar[0].blocks[0].note: A German discussion is allowed to be direct. *Das stimmt nicht* is not an insult; it’s a contribution.
grammar[0].blocks[1].title: Useful fillers
grammar[0].blocks[2].title: Streitkultur
grammar[0].blocks[2].text: A good argument is a sign of respect: it shows you took the other person seriously. Germans may fight for an hour at dinner and then ask who wants more potatoes.
grammar[0].fact: German public TV is funded by a compulsory household fee, the *Rundfunkbeitrag*, of about 18 euros a month. Every home pays, whether it has a television or not. It’s among the most hotly disputed 18 euros anywhere.

grammar[1].blocks[0].title: One fact, three ways
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: You now have seven ways to say that someone did something wrong. Six of them let that person off.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Read the news like a German
grammar[1].blocks[1].note: Each of these tells you something about who is speaking.
grammar[1].blocks[1].rows[0].a: Der Minister sagte, er sei unschuldig.
grammar[1].blocks[1].rows[3].b: And no one wants to say who.
grammar[1].fact: The word *Lügenpresse*, lying press, is a slogan with an ugly history. If you hear it, you’ve learned something about the speaker.

document.intro: The real entrance of a radio building in Berlin, from 1931. The words over the door are in old letters, made of gold. It is one of the first buildings made for radio anywhere. It has been in the hands of every kind of government since.
document.fact: The building has been home to Nazi radio, to Soviet-run radio inside the British sector, and now to Berlin’s public broadcaster. It has reported a great deal of what a great many governments said.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Say each one in the voice asked for.
reading.intro: The bench in Frau Huber’s street has become national news. She’s been invited to a talk show in Hamburg, with the mayor and a politician from Berlin. The topic: *Wem gehört die Stadt?* The red light goes on.
reading.fact: The German talk show is a serious institution, with politicians and a strict politeness that sometimes breaks down. *Lassen Sie mich ausreden* may be the most German sentence in political TV.
